lead: Machine learning turns data and experience into predictions without hand-written rules. This unit gives the vocabulary and first algorithms: learning problems, learning types, concept learning and inductive bias. After it you can state a task as a learning problem, run Find-S and candidate elimination, and explain why a model that fits training data may fail on new data.
about: This unit sets the base for machine learning. Chapter 1.1 defines learning from data and shows applications. Chapter 1.2 separates supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. Chapter 1.3 turns a task into a well-posed learning problem and a design cycle. Chapter 1.4 lists the practical issues those choices create. Chapter 1.5 reviews the linear algebra and probability needed to read models. Chapter 1.6 works through concept learning with Find-S, version spaces and candidate elimination. Chapter 1.7 explains the inductive bias that makes any learner generalize. Later units reuse these terms for regression, classification, clustering, neural networks and reinforcement learning.

chapters.idea: Machine learning is the study of programs whose performance on a task improves with experience, usually data.
chapters.depth: Definition with T, P, E: task, performance measure, experience. Data, features, labels, model, hypothesis, training and test sets. The machine learning process: collect data, prepare features, choose model, train, evaluate, deploy. Applications: spam filtering, UPI fraud checks, product recommendation, crop-yield prediction, medical screening, speech and language tasks. Some syllabi name Bayesian learning in this unit; Bayes rule, MLE and MAP are treated in Unit 3.

figure.title: From data to prediction
figure.aria: A flow from training emails through feature vectors and a learning algorithm to a model, which also receives a new email and outputs a spam prediction.

chapters.example: A spam filter is trained on 1000 emails: 200 spam and 800 not spam. The rule marks an email as spam if it contains the word lottery at least twice. On 10 test emails, the rule is right on 8. What are T, P and E? What is test accuracy? Answer: T is label an email spam or not spam; P is the fraction correct; E is the 1000 labelled emails. Accuracy is 8/10 = 0.8, or 80%.
chapters.trap: Calling any program that uses data machine learning. If rules are hand-written and do not improve from experience, it is not learning.
chapters.leave: Algorithm details of regression, classification, clustering and neural networks: Units 2 to 5.

chapters.idea: Learning types differ by the feedback available: labels, no labels, or reward.
chapters.depth: Supervised learning: labelled examples, classification for discrete labels and regression for numbers. Unsupervised learning: no labels, clustering and density estimation. Reinforcement learning: agent, state, action, reward and delayed feedback. Semi-supervised and self-supervised learning only as one-line extensions if a syllabus names them. Indian examples: IRCTC waitlist prediction, UPI fraud, crop grouping. Do not derive algorithms here.

figure.aria: A tree with machine learning at the root and three branches: supervised learning with classification and regression, unsupervised learning with clustering, and reinforcement learning with an agent.

chapters.example: Classify six tasks. (1) Predict house price from area. (2) Group 500 customers by monthly spend. (3) Teach a robot to exit a maze using +1 at the exit. (4) Label email spam from 200 labelled examples. (5) Find clusters in 1000 UPI transactions. (6) Choose a cricket shot using runs scored as reward. Answer: 1 is supervised regression, 2 is unsupervised clustering, 3 is reinforcement learning, 4 is supervised classification, 5 is unsupervised clustering, 6 is reinforcement learning. Counts: 2 supervised, 2 unsupervised, 2 reinforcement.
chapters.trap: Calling clustering classification. Classification has labels, clustering does not. Reinforcement uses rewards, not labelled correct actions.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 for task, data and model terms.
chapters.leave: Detailed regression, clustering, SVM, neural-network and Q-learning algorithms: Units 2 to 6.

chapters.idea: A learning problem is well posed when task, performance measure and experience are stated, and a learning system is designed around those three.
chapters.depth: Well-posed learning problem: T, P, E; check that a problem has all three and a clear data source. Design cycle: data collection, data preparation, feature representation, hypothesis space, learning algorithm, evaluation, deployment. Perspectives: geometric, probabilistic and logical views, one line each. Learning as search over hypotheses is introduced here and detailed in Chapter 1.6.

figure.title: Designing a learning system
figure.aria: A design flow from task T and data E through representation and algorithm to performance P and a deployed model.

chapters.example: Design a loan repayment predictor. Past records: 5000 loans, of which 500 default. T is predict repay or default; P is accuracy; E is 5000 labelled records. A model that always says repay has accuracy 4500/5000 = 90%. Why is this not a good design? Answer: the data are imbalanced; accuracy hides the default class. The design must add a target on default detection, such as recall or a cost measure.
chapters.trap: Stating only the task and forgetting P and E. Another trap is using accuracy on imbalanced data as the only performance measure.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 for features and labels; Chapter 1.2 for learning types.
chapters.leave: Full regression and model evaluation: Unit 2. Search algorithms for concept learning: Chapter 1.6.

chapters.idea: Most machine learning failures come from data and generalization problems, not from the choice of algorithm alone.
chapters.depth: Challenges: small or noisy data, missing values, imbalanced classes, overfitting and underfitting, bias-variance trade-off, curse of dimensionality, feature scaling, data leakage, concept drift and evaluation choice. Cross-reference Unit 2 for full bias-variance, regularization, cross-validation and metrics. Only a few universities teach domain shift here; define it in one line. Mention that a test set must not leak into training.

figure.aria: A plot of training error falling steadily and validation error first falling then rising as model complexity grows.

chapters.example: A polynomial model is fitted at three degrees. Degree 1: training error 0.30, validation error 0.32. Degree 3: training error 0.10, validation error 0.12. Degree 9: training error 0.01, validation error 0.45. Which is underfit, which is a good fit, and which is overfit? Answer: degree 1 underfits; degree 3 is a good fit; degree 9 overfits because training error is low but validation error is high.
chapters.trap: Judging a model by training error alone. Low training error can mean overfitting, not a better model.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.3 for the design cycle and performance measure.
chapters.leave: Bias-variance derivation, regularization and cross-validation: Unit 2. Ensemble methods: Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Linear algebra and probability give the language for features, models, uncertainty and distributions.
chapters.depth: Vectors, matrices, dot product, norms, matrix multiplication, transpose and inverse; eigenvalues only as a one-line preview for PCA. Random variables, discrete and continuous, joint, marginal and conditional probability, expectation, variance, covariance and correlation. Bernoulli, binomial, uniform and Gaussian; univariate and multivariate Gaussian. Bayes rule named but not derived; Unit 3 handles MLE, MAP and naive Bayes. Quick data exploration: mean, median, IQR, scatter plot, box plot and histogram, used to spot outliers and correlation.

figure.aria: Two bell-shaped Gaussian density curves, one centered at 0 and one centered at 1.

chapters.example: Among 1000 users, A means uses UPI and B means shops online. Counts: 400 use both, 200 use UPI only, 100 shop online only, and 300 neither. Find P(A), P(B), P(A and B) and P(B|A). Answer: P(A)=600/1000=0.60; P(B)=500/1000=0.50; P(A and B)=400/1000=0.40; P(B|A)=400/600=0.667. Since P(B|A) is not P(B), A and B are not independent.
chapters.trap: Mixing P(A|B) with P(B|A). Conditional probability is not symmetric.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 for features and data terms; school algebra.
chapters.leave: Bayes theorem, MLE, MAP, naive Bayes and Bayesian networks: Unit 3. PCA eigenvalues: Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Concept learning searches a hypothesis space for a rule that covers positive examples and rejects negative ones, using Find-S and version spaces.
chapters.depth: Concept learning task: target concept, hypothesis as a conjunction of attribute constraints, ? means any value, ∅ means no value. General-to-specific ordering. Find-S. Version space with S and G boundaries. Candidate elimination: positive examples generalize S, negative examples specialize G, then prune. List-then-eliminate as brute force. Some syllabi call the same algorithm candidate elimination. Work with small tables.

figure.aria: A small hypothesis graph: the most general hypothesis specializes to G and a removed hypothesis h, and both specialize to S; the version space lies between G and S.

chapters.example: Attributes: Sky, Temp, Wind. Positive examples: (Sunny, Warm, Strong) and (Sunny, Warm, Weak). Negative examples: (Rainy, Cold, Strong) and (Sunny, Cold, Strong). Run Find-S. Start h=(∅,∅,∅); after the first positive h=(Sunny,Warm,Strong); after the second positive h=(Sunny,Warm,?). The negatives do not change h. Final Find-S h=(Sunny,Warm,?). Candidate elimination ends with S=(Sunny,Warm,?) and G=(?,Warm,?).
chapters.trap: Generalizing S on a negative example or specializing G on a positive example. Remember: positives change S, negatives change G. Also ? is not the same as ∅.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.3 for hypothesis space and learning as search; Chapter 1.5 for sets and probability intuition.
chapters.leave: Decision tree induction and rule learning: Units 3 and 6.

chapters.idea: Inductive bias is the set of assumptions that lets a learner choose a general rule from limited data.
chapters.depth: Inductive bias: the assumptions a learner uses to choose one general rule among many consistent ones. Bias of Find-S is the most specific hypothesis. Bias of candidate elimination is the chosen hypothesis space. Bias of decision trees is a preference for shorter trees. Generalization: training error, test error and the gap between them; overfitting preview. No free lunch in one line. Probabilistic view: prior, likelihood and posterior; MAP as a bias, with full Bayes in Unit 3.

figure.title: Bias and generalization
figure.aria: A flow from training data and a hypothesis space through inductive bias to a chosen model, which is then checked on test data to measure generalization.

chapters.example: Two hypotheses h1 and h2 both fit 20 training emails with 18 correct. h1 has 30 rules; h2 has 3 rules. On 100 test emails, h1 is correct on 65 and h2 on 80. Compute training error, test error and the generalization gap. Answer: training error = 2/20 = 10% for both; test error h1 = 35%, h2 = 20%; gap h1 = 25 points, h2 = 10 points. The simpler h2 generalizes better, showing a complexity preference as inductive bias.
chapters.trap: Saying a learner has no bias. Every learner that generalizes beyond seen data has some inductive bias.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.6 for version spaces and Find-S; Chapter 1.4 for overfitting.
chapters.leave: Formal learning theory, VC dimension and full Bayesian model averaging: advanced units outside this book. Detailed Bayes and ensembles: Units 3 and 5.
